young.html: Joseph Conrad was a sailor before he was a writer. He was born to Polish parents, went to sea as a teenager, and learned English as a grown man. In 1890 he took a job steering a small steamboat up the Congo River in Africa. What he saw there shocked him, and years later he turned it into a story.

In Heart of Darkness, a sailor named Marlow sits on a boat on the River Thames at sunset and tells his friends about a journey he once made. A trading company sent him up a great African river to find Mr. Kurtz, its most famous agent. The farther Marlow travels, the more he sees how greed for ivory has made the company's men cruel to the people who live there.

young.html: For parents: this short novel is for older teens and adults. It describes the cruelty of colonial rule and uses the racial language of its time. The lesson below explains this without repeating it.

A story inside a story. Conrad's book is a story someone tells to friends. Try it: tell your family about a trip you took, but start with where you are sitting right now. Then ask: how does the teller change the story? What might the listeners never find out?

full.html: Joseph Conrad (1857–1924) was born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski to Polish parents in what is now Ukraine. He spent about twenty years at sea, became a British subject, and wrote his novels in his third language. In 1890 he worked for a Belgian company on the Congo River, in the colony then ruled personally by King Leopold II of Belgium. Heart of Darkness appeared as a magazine serial in 1899 and as a book in 1902.
Five friends wait for the tide on a yacht, the Nellie, on the Thames. As the sun goes down over London, Marlow begins:

full.text: “And this also,” said Marlow suddenly, “has been one of the dark places of the earth.”
full.author: Conrad
full.ed: Youth: A Narrative, and Two Other Stories (William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London)

full.html: He means that Britain, too, was once a wild frontier to the Romans. Then he tells how a Company in a European city (Brussels, though he never names it) hired him to captain a river steamer. Along the coast and at the Company's stations he sees forced labor, waste and cruelty, all for ivory. He hears again and again of Mr. Kurtz, a gifted agent who sends back more ivory than anyone, and he grows curious to meet him.

full.text: Going up that river was like traveling back to the earliest beginnings of the world, when vegetation rioted on the earth and the big trees were kings. An empty stream, a great silence, an impenetrable forest.
full.author: Conrad
full.ed: Youth: A Narrative, and Two Other Stories (William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London)

full.html: At the Inner Station Marlow finds that Kurtz, who left Europe full of fine words about bringing "progress," has made himself a tyrant over the people around him. Kurtz is dying. On the boat downstream he whispers his last words, "The horror! The horror!" Back in Europe, Marlow visits the woman Kurtz was engaged to and, unable to tell her the truth, tells her a kind lie.

full.html: We hear Marlow through an unnamed listener on the Nellie, so the whole tale is a story within a story. Marlow keeps saying that what he saw can't quite be put into words:

full.text: It is impossible. We live, as we dream—alone....
full.author: Conrad
full.ed: Youth: A Narrative, and Two Other Stories (William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London)

full.html: Conrad's "darkness" is not only a place. It is what can grow in anyone, Kurtz most of all, when greed and power meet no check. The book turns the language of a civilizing mission against itself.

full.text: A book that is argued over

full.html: In its day the book was read as an attack on the abuses in the Congo, which reformers such as E. D. Morel and Roger Casement were exposing at the same time. In 1975 the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe gave a famous lecture, "An Image of Africa," arguing that the book still treats Africa only as a dark backdrop for a European's crisis and denies its African people a voice. Many readers now hold both views together: the book condemns colonial greed, and it also shares some of the blind spots of its time. Its racial language is one reason it is for older readers.
Mixing up Marlow and Conrad, or Marlow and Kurtz. Marlow is the teller; Kurtz is the man he goes to find; Conrad stands behind them both.

items: Dante's Inferno, earlier on this ladder, is another journey downward into evil with a guide and a witness.
Homer's Odyssey gave the West its first great voyage tale; Conrad's is a voyage with no homecoming of the heart.
T. S. Eliot first chose Kurtz's last words for the head of The Waste Land (Ezra Pound talked him out of it), and later put the news of Kurtz's death at the head of his poem "The Hollow Men" (1925).
Chinua Achebe answered with his own novel of Africa, Things Fall Apart (1958), told from inside an Igbo village.
Why does Marlow lie at the end, when he says he hates lies? Was it right?
Can fine words about progress hide cruelty? How would you notice?
Can a book attack injustice and still share some of its age's prejudices?
What does Kurtz see when he says "The horror!"?

questions: Marlow tells his story to friends on a boat. Why do you think Conrad framed it that way?
What did the Company say it was doing in Africa, and what was it really doing?
Why do you think Kurtz changed so much?
Was Marlow's lie to Kurtz's fiancée kind, or wrong, or both?
Achebe and Conrad saw the same story very differently. How can two readers disagree about one book?
care: Describes the cruelty of colonial rule in the Congo, with violence and death, and uses the racial language of its time. For older teens and adults; the lesson summarizes without repeating that language.
